analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies and polluters to reduce disproportionate pollution burdens on communities of color and low-income communities.
analysis.headline: The Environmental Justice For All Act, backed by 78 House Democrats, got one hearing and never came to a House floor vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made environmental racism a legally recognized wrong: it would let residents sue federal agencies when agency actions have discriminatory effects on communities of color, require air and water pollution permits to account for the combined pollution already hitting a neighborhood, and deny permits to repeat violators. It also required agencies to study and involve communities before siting projects near them, labeled toxic ingredients in cosmetics and menstrual products, and funded parks, transit-to-trails access, and community grants for the neighborhoods that bear the most pollution.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of 'fenceline' communities — neighborhoods of color, low-income neighborhoods, and tribal and indigenous communities that sit next to polluting facilities — gain stronger legal tools, tighter permit standards, and new grant funding. Fossil-fuel-dependent workers and communities also gain transition assistance funded by new revenues.

how_it_helps.text: Amends Title VI of the Civil Rights Act to make discriminatory 'disparate impacts' by federal agencies illegal and gives any aggrieved person the right to sue, with attorney's fees available to prevailing plaintiffs.

Requires air and water pollution permits to ensure a 'reasonable certainty of no harm' considering cumulative impacts from all pollution sources in the area, and requires repeat violators to submit compliance plans or lose their permits.

Requires federal agencies preparing environmental reviews to assess combined and cumulative health hazards on affected communities, hold hearings in the community in local languages, and translate documents into languages spoken by more than 5% of residents.

Creates grant programs for community groups, requires ingredient labeling on cosmetics and menstrual products, funds research into safer chemical alternatives, and directs a share of Gulf of Mexico energy revenues to urban park grants plus $10 million a year for transit-to-trails access.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that operate or seek air and water permits near these communities — power plants, refineries, manufacturers — would face stricter cumulative-impact standards, permit denials, and compliance plans. Cosmetics and consumer product makers would face labeling mandates. Taxpayers fund the new grant programs.

drawbacks.text: Park and trail grants require local matching funds equal to the federal grant (waivable at the Secretary's discretion), which could exclude exactly the under-resourced cities the program targets.

The cumulative-impact permit standard ('reasonable certainty of no harm') and the new private right of action would make industrial permitting slower and more litigious — the strongest good-faith objection from regulated industries, which argued the standard is hard to meet and invites lawsuits.
The bill lets agency heads petition the President for exemptions from its requirements, a potential escape valve that community groups would have to monitor and appeal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health stakes are real: pollution burdens concentrate geographically, and the bill attacks them directly by changing who has to prove what — polluters and agencies, not residents. The costs fall mostly on regulated industries in compliance and litigation, though slower permitting and the 100% grant match are genuine downsides, and the presidential exemption path slightly undercuts the bill's own enforcement scheme.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to six committees, it got one hearing in October 2020, and no committee ever advanced it or the House voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill on February 27, 2020 with 19 original cosponsors including Rep. Donald McEachin.

The Speaker referred it to six committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, Judiciary, Transportation and Infrastructure, Agriculture, and Education and Labor — splitting it across jurisdictions.
Part of the bill was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security on March 10, 2020.
The full Natural Resources Committee held one hearing on October 1, 2020; no markup or floor action followed.
Seventy-seven House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans cosponsored.
The bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with no vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Emitting industries and consumer product makers are better off: they face no cumulative-impact permitting standards, no repeat-violator permit denials, and no new ingredient labeling mandates. Fenceline communities, which had 78 House sponsors behind the bill, gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All 78 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats — none of the chamber's 197 Republicans signed on — and the Democratic-controlled House never brought the bill to a vote.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel and industrial emitters (power plants, refineries, manufacturers)
industries.note: The bill would require permit decisions to weigh the combined pollution already in a neighborhood and to deny or condition permits for repeat violators, directly threatening facility siting and expansion near these communities. Its gain — fewer permit constraints — is the community's continued exposure.

Mandatory ingredient labeling on cosmetics and menstrual products and research into safer chemical alternatives would impose compliance costs, while the public gains disclosure about toxic ingredients in everyday products.
New grant programs for community capacity building, park access, and safer products would channel federal money to grassroots organizations in affected neighborhoods.
